item.title: We are losing the fight against dengue. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
With 518 confirmed deaths as of writing this editorial and fast approaching 175,000 hospitalizations recorded so far this year, marking the third-deadliest outbreak in Bangladesh’s history, our response to dengue remains inadequate, to say the least.
Why such a response has descended from disappointing to outright infuriating is because three years after the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) drafted the National Dengue Prevention and Control Strategy (2024-2030), virtually zero tangible progress is visible on the ground.
Dengue has long been far more than an unpredictable seasonal anomaly and rather an annual public health emergency. Yet, the battle against dengue is one Bangladesh continues to lose because of chronic administrative incompetence.
As prominent entomologists and public health experts have rightly pointed out, the national strategy itself is fundamentally flawed, allegedly drafted behind closed doors by bureaucrats without input from entomologists or field specialists, rendering it unscientific and detached from reality.
Worse still, even the basic directives within that document remain unexecuted. Year-round destruction of Aedes breeding grounds is nonexistent, coordination between the health ministry and local government bodies remains broken, and disease surveillance misses countless cases treated or lost at home.
Equally inexcusable is the continued centralization of treatment. By failing to equip district and upazila hospitals with adequate diagnostic kits, skilled personnel, and intensive care capacity, authorities force critically ill patients from across the country to undertake perilous journeys to Dhaka, overwhelming capital hospitals.
Bureaucratic inertia continues costing innocent citizens their lives. If the government wants to demonstrate that it truly cares about people’s suffering, then it must immediately overhaul its failed approach. We cannot keep treating preventable deaths as inevitable statistics.

item.title: Execution is everything for development projects. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The 16 recent development projects approved by the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (Ecnec) worth Tk33,298.48 crore, of which less than Tk500cr will be from external sources, is certainly an ambitious push to strengthen rural connectivity, revive dying waterways, and bolster agricultural productivity.
From constructing 256 long rural bridges to excavating nearly 8,900 kilometres of canals, small rivers, and waterbodies across 444 upazilas, we can admire the scope and scale of these initiatives and can recognize that they target genuine developmental needs.
Building pillar-free bridges that protect natural river flows while linking remote communities, alongside restoring surface water irrigation across 2.65 lakh hectares of farmland, could deliver lasting economic and ecological dividends. These are interventions that are necessary for future prosperity.
With that said, Bangladesh’s development landscape is full of well-intentioned infrastructure schemes ruined by bad planning and worse implementation as a result of corrupt practices.
At a moment when public finances are stretched razor-thin amid severe revenue shortfalls, high inflation, and mounting debt obligations, every single taka is precious. As such, we have zero margin for waste, vanity spending, or bureaucratic lethargy.
Equally important is ensuring full safety before the project is greenlit for the implementation stage. To that end, that there remain dozens of bridges which still have not undergone feasibility studies does not inspire confidence, and must be addressed promptly. Approving massive construction packages before completing rigorous hydrological surveys and engineering assessments is a recipe for disaster.
If these projects are to succeed, the government must enforce ironclad fiscal and operational discipline from day one. Beyond ensuring the bridges requiring feasibility studies undergo thorough, independent technical evaluations, strict timelines and fixed budget ceilings must be enforced, along with penalties for contractors and project directors who manufacture artificial delays to inflate costs.
Approving projects has always merely been the starting line. It is disciplined, corruption-free execution that has eluded us.

item.title: School should be the safest space for every learner. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A mocking laugh in class, a hurtful message forwarded online or silence when a classmate is harassed can make students afraid to return to school. Every child in Bangladesh has the right to walk through the school gate free from fear. Protecting that right takes work throughout the school year. Every secondary school should have trained staff, clear procedures to prevent violence, and respond when students report it.
Globally, about one in three students reports being bullied. Estimates put the share of children affected by cyberbullying at around one in ten . Harm can be amplified online through image-based abuse and sexual extortion. Girls and boys can face different forms of violence, and poverty and disability can increase the risks. Fear can make it harder for students to learn even when they are in class.
Bangladesh has made gains in girls’ enrolment. Today, girls are enrolling in secondary schools at higher rates than boys. Yet many leave before completing Grade 10 .
The latest 2022 Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey found that about half of women aged 20 to 24 years had married before the age of 18. In the most recent 2024 Violence Against Women Survey , about 62% of ever-married girls aged 15 to 19 years reported experiencing intimate partner violence in the preceding year. Schools and communities both have a role in addressing the pressures girls face beyond the classroom.
A situation analysis on Health Promoting Schools , published in 2026 by the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE) with Unesco’s support, surveyed 458 students and 206 teachers across the country. Only 30.1% of teachers reported having received training in health education or well-being.
The study suggested that health topics receive limited classroom time partly because they are not examined. Schools can build on that support by involving families in work on safety and well-being.
The Health Promoting Schools approach makes health and well-being part of how schools teach and operate. By 2021, more than 90 countries and territories had adopted the initiative and the global Health Promoting Schools (HPS) standards and indicators published by WHO and Unesco.
Unesco’s Education for Health and Well-being strategy links healthy school systems with age-appropriate life skills and health education with learning environments free from violence and bullying. The 2023 Unesco Recommendation on Education for Peace, Human Rights and Sustainable Development identifies the safety, health, and well-being of learners and education personnel as a guiding principle. It calls for strengthening the school system to support students’ physical and mental health.
Since 2024, DSHE and the National Academy for Educational Management (NAEM), with Unesco’s support, have been piloting HPS in 30 schools in urban and rural areas of Bangladesh. The pilot has generated evidence, adapted the standards and indicators for Bangladesh and developed a competency-based curriculum for teachers, delivered through master trainers. Alongside DSHE’s Learning Acceleration in Secondary Education (LAISE) project and its cyberbullying training, it has supported reporting through complaint boxes and school anti-sexual harassment committees.
We call on government, development partners, and communities to extend this work to every secondary school, starting where need is greatest. The Health Promoting Schools standards adapted for Bangladesh can serve as a national benchmark. Each school should have a code of conduct, a complaint box, and a committee responsible for school safety.
A complaint box gives a student a way to speak up. What happens after a report determines whether that student gets help. Schools should be able to refer students confidentially to health, psychosocial, social, and legal services.
Education, health, social welfare, and law enforcement agencies should plan together so schools know where to turn. Union parishads and upazilas can help make school surroundings safer.
Teacher training should cover the skills set out in the HPS approach, including positive discipline and digital safety. Prioritize government and rural schools, where the study found teachers had received less training.
The curriculum and textbooks should teach students how to recognize and respond to online abuse, protect their privacy, and use the internet responsibly. Parents and teachers need these skills too, so they can support children when harm occurs online.
Families, religious and community leaders, and young people have a role in changing the norms that sustain child marriage. When a girl or boy drops out, schools and communities should follow up and help that learner return.
Schools should assess safety each year, plan and carry out improvements, then monitor and review progress. They should track violence, attendance, and dropout alongside the HPS indicators and learning outcomes. Pilot schools can share what works, and the findings can inform Bangladesh’s reporting under Unesco’s 2023 Recommendation.
Bangladesh’s promise of an education for every child must be kept in the classroom, on the way to school and in the online spaces children use. When a student can speak up about harm, receive support, and return to learning in safety, that promise is being put into practice.
Professor Dr Khan Moinuddin Al Mahmud Sohel , Director General, Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education. Professor Dr Wasim Md Mazbahul Haque , Director General, National Academy for Educational Management. Dr Susan Vize, Head of Office and Unesco Representative to Bangladesh.

item.title: Why cancel culture will never stick in Bangladesh. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Walk past any cha-er dokan in Dhaka on a humid evening and you will witness the true theatre of Bangladeshi public opinion.
One week, the table is united in righteous fury over a global brand, a viral clip, or a celebrity’s court-premises clash.
Voices rise, thumbs fly across cracked screens, and solemn pledges of permanent ostracization are made.
Two weeks later, the exact same crowd is arguing about cricket selections, inflation, or the next three-second clip to cross their feeds, reaching without a second thought for whatever they had just sworn off.
Cancel culture -- that distinctly Western export built on moral registries, algorithmic pile-ons, and long-memoried corporate or career exile -- never quite survives the journey to Bangladesh.
Not because Bangladeshis lack passion. Quite the opposite: We have passion in industrial quantities.
The problem is our attention span, our social fabric, and a deeply ingrained cultural habit of moving on before the kettle has even stopped whistling.
The anatomy of a thirty-day boycott
Consider the wave of consumer anger directed at Coca-Cola in Bangladesh following the escalation of the Gaza war and the backlash over its local advertising missteps.
For a stretch, boycotting multinational brands felt like a moral badge worn across timelines, with local alternatives like Mojo and RC Cola enjoying a visible surge of patriotic goodwill.
Yet retail realities in Bangladesh are notoriously stubborn.
Convenience, price points, distribution muscle, and sheer habit have a way of eroding ideological resolutions once the peak of a news cycle passes.
Even when a campaign dents sales or forces a PR scramble, turning a burst of moral indignation into permanent market erasure requires sustained discipline -- something mass outrage rarely maintains once life’s daily pressures resume.
The same short half-life shows up in celebrity and media flashpoints. Take the recurring storm around actress Pori Moni and her volatile clashes with journalists -- from heated exchanges and allegations of phone-snatching around court appearances to live-streamed accusations of "terrorism in the name of journalism."
Journalists’ associations have called protests or boycotts, commentators have dissected every angle, and social media has briefly crowned winners and villains.
Yet in Bangladesh’s entertainment and tabloid ecosystem, outrage and publicity are often Siamese twins.
A figure who is "cancelled" in one clip can re-emerge in another viral moment days later, carried forward by the very curiosity that fuelled the condemnation.
From 1990s print panics to 2020s timeline storms
Fickleness is not a gift bestowed solely on smartphones; it is an old habit wearing new clothes.
In the 1990s, as private newspapers, FM radio, and satellite television began opening up Bangladesh’s media landscape, public panics and moral outrages already moved in brisk cycles -- whether around sensational crime coverage, shifting political slogans, or cultural debates over foreign television and music.
Back then, distance and slower print cycles meant a controversy had to work harder to travel, and once the next edition hit the stands, yesterday’s scandal was already losing oxygen.
By the 2010s and 2020s, Facebook and short-form video turned that slow burn into instant wildfire.
Over the last decade and a half, Bangladesh has seen countless online storms: Sudden boycotts of specific TV dramas or advertisers, fierce pile-ons against influencers and public figures, and rapid shifts in what the entire nation is "definitely not watching or buying anymore."
History has shown that social media in Bangladesh can power massive real-world mobilization when grievances run deep and structural -- as seen during the student-led anti-discrimination uprising -- but ordinary cultural "cancelling" rarely holds.
Most online boycotts here behave less like court sentences and more like monsoon rain: Loud, dramatic, impossible to ignore for an hour, and quickly soaked into the pavement.
Across borders and back home
Zoom out across South Asia and the wider world, and you see why this pattern looks so familiar. Across South Asia, Bollywood and regional film industries have repeatedly faced hashtag boycotts -- sometimes hurting an opening weekend or two, only for audiences to return whenever a film’s buzz or star power hits the right chord.
In the West, where cancel culture is often treated as an inescapable social guillotine, even high-profile cancellations frequently turn out to be porous: Audiences split, algorithms move on to fresh targets, and figures with loyal niches often claw back visibility or reinvent themselves.
If cancel culture struggles to stay rigid even in societies built around individualist branding and HR-style accountability, it stands even less chance in Bangladesh.
Western cancel culture thrives on a tidy moral ledger: You cross a line, the crowd withdraws its patronage, and institutions enforce the exile.
Bangladesh does not run on tidy ledgers.
Our social life is dense, relational, and forgiving in ways that are both generous and frustrating.
Personal ties, addas , kinship networks, political alignments, and economic survival constantly cut across neat moral lines.
What looks like an unbreakable boycott on a Monday morning often dissolves into pragmatism -- or plain boredom -- by Friday afternoon.
Why we never quite stay mad
There is also a quieter truth behind our fickle-mindedness: Living in Bangladesh already demands a high daily quota of outrage.
Between traffic, rising living costs, workplace stress, and constant political or civic noise, nobody has the emotional bandwidth to stay furious at a soda brand or an actress’s press-scrum temper forever.
None of this means public criticism in Bangladesh is pointless.
Calling out bad ads, holding public figures accountable, or questioning corporate behaviour matters when it sparks real debate.
But expecting a Western-style cancel culture to permanently erase people or products in Bangladesh is misreading the room.
Here, the crowd rarely holds a grudge long enough to finish the sentence -- because by then, another notification has already lit up the screen.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.
